verified_metadata.title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
verified_metadata.venue: Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 70

metadata_sources.supports: Exact title, ordered authors, ICML 2017, volume 70 and pages 3319–3328.

artifact.version_note: Official ICML 2017 proceedings PDF; title and all authors checked on p. 1.

contexts.evidence: Sections 2–3 develop Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance as axioms and derive Integrated Gradients; the attribution-family description is accurate.

Sections 2.1 and 3 (PDF pp. 2–3) confirm IG is axiomatic but explicitly explain how baseline/discrete-gradient methods and IG overcome local saturation. Thus the paragraph's claim of structural loss for every backward-pass method is broader than the cited evidence.
contexts.proposed_replacement: This section identifies a structural information loss that the original graph inflicts on ordinary local-gradient attribution, and shows that the split-pair representation of Section~\ref{sec:dc_splitting_relu} removes it.

contexts.evidence: Section 2.1 (PDF p. 2) gives exactly f(x)=1−ReLU(1−x), x=2, baseline 0, and zero ordinary-gradient attribution. It does not establish zero attribution for every local backward rule: the same section discusses DeepLIFT's discrete-gradient remedy.
contexts.proposed_replacement: The prediction changes, $f(2) - f(0) = 1 - 0 = 1$, so the single feature is plainly relevant; yet $f$ is constant on $x \geq 1$, so the gradient at $x = 2$ --- and with it Input$\times$Gradient and backward rules that retain the original local ReLU derivatives --- assigns exactly zero attribution.

contexts.evidence: Section 2.1 states Sensitivity(a): if input and baseline differ in one feature and prediction, that feature must receive nonzero attribution. The following thesis definition matches this axiom.

Section 3 defines the straight-line gradient integral relative to a baseline; Section 6.1 (PDF p. 6) uses a black image with all pixel intensities zero. This supports the described IntGrad baseline, while actual experiment settings remain the thesis's implementation claim.

notes: Nearby uncited sentence in 05_saliency.tex describing subthreshold loss as affecting every attribution method on the original graph is also too broad. DeepLIFT and IG are counterexamples to this universal formulation; scope the claim to ordinary input gradients or methods that preserve the local ReLU derivative.

verified_metadata.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale

metadata_sources.supports: Exact title, all 12 ordered authors, identifier and camera-ready version statement.
Official ICLR 2021 listing includes this paper.

artifact.version_note: arXiv:2010.11929v2 (3 June 2021), identified by arXiv as the ICLR camera-ready version with two small corrections; PDF p. 1 explicitly says published at ICLR 2021.

contexts.evidence: Sections 3.1 and 4 (PDF pp. 3–5) describe non-overlapping patch tokens and the /16 size notation. This reference supports the ViT architecture clause; grid-artifact findings belong to the co-cited DAVE paper.

Section 3.1, Inductive bias (PDF p. 4), contrasts CNN translation equivariance with ViT; Section 4 explains /16 means 16×16 input patches. The grid-artifact attribution is supplied by the adjacent Wrobel2024 citation, rather than demonstrated here.

Section 4/Table 1 (PDF p. 5), and the Appendix B results identify the ViT-Base architecture and ViT-B/16 variant. This establishes the backbone identity; checkpoint and dataset details are separate experiment provenance.
Section 4/Table 1 (PDF p. 5) and Appendix B describe ViT-Base and the /16 patch variant, supporting the named evaluated architecture; the conditioned game is the thesis's own method.

notes: The original paper supports patch tokenization, variant names and lack of CNN-style translation equivariance. It does not itself study attribution-grid artifacts; that portion of the mixed citation must be supported by Wrobel2024. ViTs in general need not use 16×16 patches; this is correct for the evaluated ViT-B/16.

verified_metadata.title: The Atlas of In-Context Learning: How Attention Heads Shape In-Context Retrieval Augmentation
verified_metadata.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025)

metadata_sources.supports: Official proceedings establish ordered authors, exact title, NeurIPS 2025 volume 38 and DOI.
Matching preprint identity, arXiv:2505.15807.

artifact.version_note: Official NeurIPS 2025 proceedings PDF, 45 pages, with matching title and all five authors on p. 1.

contexts.evidence: Sections 5–6 (pp. 5–9) use AttnLRP to distinguish in-context and parametric heads, further separate task and retrieval heads, and validate functional roles through ablation, function vectors and attention-weight interventions.

Sections 5–6 localize attention-head roles using relevance scores and intervene on identified heads; this supports attribution-based head identification and downstream control. The final statement about unstable attributions is a thesis inference, not an empirical result claimed by this paper.

Sections 5–6 identify heads from attribution and show effects of targeted ablations, function-vector insertion and attention-weight changes on answer generation; the head-identification/control claim is supported.

notes: Existing abbreviated NeurIPS venue and year are correct; the verified metadata above supplies the official proceedings URL and DOI if enrichment is desired.

verified_metadata.title: Convex Analysis Approach to D. C. Programming: Theory, Algorithms and Applications

metadata_sources.supports: Official journal PDF first page confirms full ordered authors, title, Acta Mathematica Vietnamica 22(1), 1997, pp. 289–355.

artifact.version_note: Official published article; 67 pages, printed pp. 289–355. Title and author list read from extracted first page.

contexts.evidence: Section 2, pp. 294–297, develops DC functions and closure under linear combinations and finite maxima; p. 296 explicitly gives the positive-part split max(g,h)-h for f=g-h. These facts supply classical background for a recursive ReLU DC split. The article studies DC optimization rather than neural attribution.

notes: No DOI shown in the official journal record or PDF. The paper discusses numerical stability of DCA choices (e.g. p. 291), but not cancellation instability in the neural-network split referred to by the thesis.
